messages.author: f20e19f0f77c5e8e
messages.subject: Covariates in MCDS
parts:
Hello all,

I'm analyzing point transect data for songbirds and I would like to evaluate observer and day of year as covariates into the detection function.  Ive had no problems incorporating observer as a factor variable in my analysis however when I incorporate day of year (julien date) as a non factor covariate in the observation layer I cant get the analysis to work.. This is the warning I get:

** Error: Analysis engine terminated unexpectedly (with error code -1073741663).  **
 ** Internal Error 53: Mismatched modules -            2           0           0
           0  **
 ** Internal Error 54: Mismatched stats -            4           0           0
           0           2  **
  For background, I chose 1-3 random locations for point counts at 190 restored patches.  We visited the points between 1-4 times during the breeding season.  To estimate density, I'm post stratifying using the stratum layer and easement is the field name with sample layer used for the encounter rate.

Any help/advice you may have would be greatly appreciated.  Ive attached a screenshot of the data in Distance and a sample spreadsheet of the original data for your convenience.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariates in MCDS
parts:
Bryan:

I don't have a complete answer for you regarding the specific error messages you received.  However, I did do a quick summary of the dataset you supplied and produced this table of number of sighting by date and observer:

 date AKW BR CL
  139   0  0 10
  151   0 30  0
  157   0  0 13
  173   0 33  0
  181  26  0  0
  191   0 26  0
  203   0 16  0

I think any model that contained both date and observer would struggle because the two predictors are confounded with one another; e.g. were there more detections on day 139 because it was early in the season or because "CL" made the detections; cannot be resolved.

Moral of the story:  know what you are asking Distance to do before making the request.  Know your data well (by looking at summaries, tables, graphs) before beginning to fit detection functions.
